headline: Forget the Fluke — The Bunker Blitz Just Showed Up at the Inlet
subhead: While half the bay is still soaking Gulp for stray fluke, the real show is bass and blues hammering bunker pods right at the mouth of Jones Inlet.
body_markdown:
Every tackle shop conversation this week starts the same way — guys asking where the fluke went. Wrong question. The fluke bite in Sloop Channel and around the Wantagh Bridge flats has been thinning out for two weeks now, and that's not a mystery, that's the calendar. What nobody's talking about enough is what's happening twenty yards off the beach at the inlet mouth, where bunker pods have been stacking thick enough to turn the water black, and bass and blues have finally committed to them. We flagged this coming — said the building tide would tighten those pods and trigger the first real blitz of the season right at the inlet mouth, and that's exactly what's playing out now.

Here's the why, and it's not complicated. The ocean's been ugly — close to four-foot swell out there, short and choppy, with water pushing past 71 degrees on the outside buoys. That kind of slop doesn't kill the bite, it relocates it. Bass and bluefish don't want to sit out in that washing machine any more than you'd want to fish it comfortably. So everything — bait and predators both — gets squeezed into the calmer, structured water inside the inlet and along the jetty rocks at Short Beach. The bunker have nowhere to hide, and the stripers and blues know it. That's your blitz.

The pattern right now is tide-dependent, and it's not an all-day thing — don't let anybody tell you it is. The best window has been the last two hours of the outgoing, when the current rips out of the back bay and funnels bait straight through the inlet throat. That's when the bunker get disorganized, balled up tight against the north side of the channel, and that's when you'll hear the surface explode. Guys working the jetty at Short Beach with topwater — Super Strike Little Neck poppers and 7-inch Yo-Zuri darters in bunker patterns — have had legit shots at bass in the mid-20s to low-30s, plus bluefish running 4 to 8 pounds that are hitting like freight trains and leaving half the plug behind. If you're throwing metal, a 2-ounce Kastmaster or a Deadly Dick in silver covers the strike zone fast when the blitz is moving, which it does — sometimes fifty yards down the beach in a matter of minutes.

Boat guys working right off Jones Beach have been snagging bunker with weighted trebles and drifting them back on a fish-finder rig, no weight or just enough to keep it down 10 to 15 feet, letting the current do the work along the edge of the pod. That's produced the better bass — a few overslot fish reported in that 34-to-38-inch class — along with bluefish thick enough that some boats are cutting the trip short just from the toll on tackle and hooks. The bite isn't a guarantee every drift. It's been more binary than that — dead water for twenty minutes, then five rods bent at once when the pod gets pinned against structure. That's early fall inlet fishing. You put in the time on the right tide or you don't get the window at all.

Don't sleep on the night bite at Wantagh Bridge either. Weakfish have been showing up again in the bay after a few lean years, and the bridge lights at night on the last of the ebb have been holding them along with schoolie bass. Small white or chartreuse bucktails, quarter-ounce, tipped with a strip of squid or a 3-inch Gulp shrimp, worked slow right along the shadow line — that's the ticket. Nobody's filling a cooler with weakfish yet, but seeing them at all after this long is worth paying attention to, and it tells you the bay's health is trending the right direction.

Fluke guys aren't totally out of luck — there are still keepers to be had drifting bucktail-and-Gulp combinations in the deeper bends of Sloop Channel on the last of the incoming, especially around the Wantagh Bridge pilings where the current holds bait longer. But the size and numbers are both fading fast as those fish start their exit toward the ocean. If fluke is all you care about, this is closing-week fishing, not peak-season fishing.

Looking at the next few days, the moon's building toward full, which means bigger tidal swings and more water moving through the inlet — that's good news for concentrating bait even further. If the ocean lays down at all, expect some of that bunker to push back out past the jetty tips, which could open up a surf bite right off the sand at Jones Beach proper, not just inside the inlet. If it stays sloppy out there, stick to the inlet mouth and Short Beach rocks on the outgoing — that's been the honest, repeatable window all week. Either way, the bunker aren't leaving yet, and as long as they're here, the bass and blues will keep showing up to eat them. This is the start of the fall run, not the peak of it — the next two weeks should only get better as more bait gets pushed out of the back bay and the water keeps cooling.
